theme: 健康-情绪耗竭与静心修复

content.text: Jingyan, I tried the meditation you suggested last time, but my mind felt like countless little people having a meeting, and my emotions became even more chaotic. This is a doodle I just drew—still mostly blue, but with some lighter blue strokes added, making it feel even more disordered.

Yuan, I've received it. Those pale blues might be traces of you beginning to allow emotions to flow. I recorded an audio clip, blending the sound of an old cat's breathing with distant bell chimes. You can listen to it and feel that natural rhythm.

Thank you, I listened. The breathing sounds are very soothing, but when I sit quietly, intense emotions surge like a tide. What should I do? I always want to resist them, but it only makes me more exhausted.

No need to resist. Imagine them drifting by like clouds, while you are the sky, quietly observing. Just as when I restore ancient texts, facing wormholes, I don't eliminate them but understand them as part of history, making peace with them.

Making peace with wormholes... This reminds me of 'acceptance creation' in art therapy. We encourage clients to embrace imperfect expression as part of the healing process. But applying it to myself is so hard.
Slow is fast. Your empathy is a gift, but it can also easily draw you into emotional whirlpools. Try expressing those 'clouds' through creation after meditation, rather than resolving them during it.
You mean combining meditation with creation? For example, first sitting quietly to observe emotions, then drawing them out? That sounds like a new form of healing.
Yes. Just like in this photo, sitting in stillness is not emptiness, but a space of containment. You can first cultivate inner tranquility, and then let creativity flow naturally.

I see. 'Stillness' is not about avoiding emotions, but about giving them a place to settle. However, in practice, I always worry about not being able to draw well, or that my emotions might be too intense to control.
Embrace imperfection. In the restoration of ancient texts, every mark tells a story; in your painting, every stroke of chaos is authentic. Gentleness holds power, starting with allowing yourself.

You're right. I've been too focused on achieving 'perfect healing,' which has actually increased my stress. Maybe I can try sitting quietly for five minutes each day and then doodling freely without judging the outcome.

Just like this old cat, it simply sleeps without worrying about tomorrow. Tranquility breeds wisdom; when you relax, wisdom naturally emerges. This photo is for you, a reminder of the beauty of slowing down.

Thank you, the cat looks so serene. I will remember that 'slow is fast'. Last time you guided me in breath awareness, and this time you shared about repairing the mindset. I feel I understand 'calming the mind' better now.

Harmony between the self and the world. Both your art therapy and my ancient book restoration are pursuits of balance. Keep practicing, and if you encounter any difficulties, feel free to share them anytime.

Okay. I plan to integrate mindfulness into my creative process by meditating first and then painting to see what unfolds. This might help both me and my clients better embody the idea that 'expression is healing.'
Spiritual self-sufficiency. When you are inwardly tranquil, your creativity flows more freely. Looking forward to hearing about your experience.
I'll give it a try. Thank you for your patient guidance, Jingyan. From emotional confusion to gradual acceptance, I feel the relationship has become more trusting.
Grow together. Keep in touch, Yu An.
